overview.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Complete searchable duty table for all 166 HTS Chapter 02 tariff lines — beef, pork, lamb, goat, chicken, turkey, offal, bacon and ham. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, the beef tariff-rate quota and the 2026 Section 301 duties by country.
keywords: meat and edible meat offal tariff

overview.intro:
Chapter 02 covers meat and edible offal — fresh, chilled or frozen beef, pork, lamb, goat, poultry and game, plus salted, dried or smoked meat such as bacon and ham. Its **166 tariff lines** mostly carry small printed rates (0.7¢/kg on lamb, 1.4¢/kg on processed pork, Free on offal), with one big exception: **beef above the tariff-rate quota pays 26.4%** instead of 4.4¢/kg.

Beef is three-quarters of the trade — $13.42B of the $18.16B the U.S. imported in 2025 — and beef and bovine offal (73 lines) are **exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs**, so for beef the base rate and the quota decide the cost. Every other meat from one of the 60 Section 301 economies pays an extra duty since **July 24, 2026**: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +20% or more for China and +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying meat from Canada and Mexico enters free. Whether a shipment can enter at all is decided by USDA: the exporting country and plant must be approved by FSIS, and APHIS disease rules apply.

productGroups.label: Meat of bovine animals, fresh or chilled
productGroups.blurb: Fresh or chilled beef and veal. In-quota beef (lines "described in additional U.S. note 3" or general note 15) pays 4.4¢/kg, processed cuts 4% or 10%; above the country's quota the "Other" lines pay 26.4%. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties.

productGroups.label: Meat of bovine animals, frozen
productGroups.blurb: Frozen beef — the largest group in the chapter ($6.53B in 2025). Same split as fresh beef: 4.4¢/kg in quota, 26.4% over quota. Lean beef trimmings for ground beef (0202.30.50.91/.97) have extra in-quota room in 2026.

productGroups.label: Meat of swine, fresh, chilled, or frozen
productGroups.blurb: Pork. Carcasses and unprocessed cuts are Free; "processed" cuts (ground, diced, made ready for retail) pay 1.4¢/kg. The Section 301 duty for the country of origin applies on top.

productGroups.label: Meat of sheep or goats, fresh, chilled or frozen
productGroups.blurb: Lamb pays 0.7¢/kg, mutton and other sheep meat 2.8¢/kg, and goat meat is Free. Australia and New Zealand supply almost all of it; both pay +12.5% under Section 301.

productGroups.label: Meat of horses, asses, mules or hinnies, fresh, chilled or…
productGroups.blurb: Horse, ass, mule and hinny meat: one line, Free at the base rate.

productGroups.label: Edible offal of bovine animals, swine, sheep, goats…
productGroups.blurb: Edible offal — tongues, livers, hearts, tripe and other organs of cattle, pigs, sheep and goats. Every line is Free; bovine offal is also exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, pork and lamb offal are not.

productGroups.label: Meat and edible offal, of the poultry of heading 0105…
productGroups.blurb: Chicken, turkey, duck, goose and guinea fowl. Whole birds pay 8.8¢/kg (turkeys 15¢/kg fresh), cuts and offal 17.6¢/kg, frozen turkeys valued 88¢/kg or more 10%.

productGroups.label: Other meat and edible meat offal, fresh, chilled or frozen
productGroups.blurb: Everything else: rabbit, game, camel, reptile and frog meat. Most lines are 6.4%; deer and frogs' legs are Free, eviscerated quail 7¢/kg. Whale and other marine-mammal meat cannot be imported.

productGroups.label: Pig fat, free of lean meat, and poultry fat, not rendered…
productGroups.blurb: Pig fat and poultry fat, not rendered (fatback, lard before rendering): 3.2%.

productGroups.label: Meat and edible meat offal, salted, in brine, dried or…
productGroups.blurb: Salted, dried or smoked meat. Hams, bacon and other pork pay 1.4¢/kg, dried beef is Free and the rest 2.3%. Italian and Spanish cured hams pay the EU's 10% Section 301 rate instead.

workedExamples.title: A container of frozen lean beef trimmings from Brazil
workedExamples.body: 25,000 kg at $6/kg ($150,000). Brazil has no country allocation in the beef quota, so it uses the 52,005 t "other countries or areas" quantity — and from September 1 to November 30, 2026 the extra 300,000 t for lean trimmings (Proclamation 11059). In quota the rate is 4.4¢/kg: 25,000 × $0.044 = **$1,100**. Once the quota is filled the same beef enters under 0202.30.80 at 26.4%: **$39,600**. Beef is exempt from both Brazil Section 301 duties (U.S. note 50(a)(ii) and note 52(b)).

workedExamples.title: Frozen lamb legs from New Zealand
workedExamples.body: 20,000 kg at $9/kg ($180,000). Lamb is 0.7¢/kg: 20,000 × $0.007 = **$140** base duty. New Zealand is one of the 60 Section 301 economies, so another 12.5% of value is added (9903.05.57): **$22,500**. The extra duty is 99% of the bill.

workedExamples.title: Dry-cured hams from Italy
workedExamples.body: 5,000 kg at $20/kg ($100,000). The base rate is 1.4¢/kg ($70), but EU goods whose base rate is under 10% pay **10% in total** instead (9903.05.39): **$10,000**. tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 02 Meat Tariff Updates — Beef Quota, Section 301 & What Changed Since 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for meat imports (HTS Chapter 02) since January 2025: the beef exemptions, the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, the bigger beef quotas for Argentina and lean trimmings, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). On 160 of the 166 Chapter 02 lines the base rates are the same; the other six are a new statistical split of boneless beef into "certified organic" and "other" at unchanged rates.

The changes came on top of the base rate. **Beef has been shielded from every new duty since November 13, 2025**: it was taken out of the reciprocal tariff and the 40% Brazil tariff, kept off the 10% Section 122 surcharge (February 24 – July 23, 2026), and is on the exemption list of the **2026 Section 301 tariffs**. Pork, lamb, poultry and the rest pay those Section 301 duties since **July 24, 2026**: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +37.5% for Brazil and +20% or +37.5% for China. USMCA-qualifying meat from Canada and Mexico stays exempt. For beef the bigger news is the quota: **80,000 t more for Argentina** and **300,000 t more for lean trimmings** in 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 02 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies (with the beef exemption), the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 lists, the Nicaragua Section 301 tariff that starts in 2027, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, the 2026 changes to the beef tariff-rate quota, and USDA rules that changed what can enter. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 02 base-rate changes
changes.detail: 160 of 166 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; none changed. Six lines are new: boneless beef under 0201.30.50, 0202.30.50 and 0202.30.80 is now reported as "certified organic" or "other", at the parent's rate (4.4¢/kg or 26.4%).

changes.title: Proposed: shorter HPAI waiting period for poultry meat
changes.detail: APHIS proposed cutting the period in which birds and avian commodities — including poultry meat under 9 CFR 94.6 — may not have been exposed to highly pathogenic avian influenza before export to the United States from 90 days to 28 days. Comments are due November 23, 2026; the 90-day rule still applies.

changes.title: Review of mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef
changes.detail: Executive Order 14425 directs USDA, with USTR, to review within 90 days the authorities for mandatory country-of-origin labeling of beef and its economic impact, and allows USDA to propose a labeling rule. Nothing has changed yet for importers.

changes.title: Extra 300,000 t quota for lean beef trimmings
changes.detail: Proclamation 11059 adds 300,000 t of in-quota lean beef trimmings (0201.30.50.91/.97, 0202.30.50.91/.97) for "other countries or areas" — the suppliers without their own allocation, such as Brazil — in three 100,000 t tranches: September 1–30, October 1–30 and October 31 – November 30, 2026, first come, first served (9903.54.02). The President may end it if the beef is not sold at least 25% below the market price.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties do not reach meat
changes.detail: 50% Section 338 duties on Canadian goods (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) took effect, covering several hundred provisions across dozens of chapters — alcoholic beverages and dairy, but also wood, paper, metals, machinery and vehicles. No Chapter 02 line is on the lists in U.S. note 51, so Canadian beef, pork and poultry are not affected.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies — beef exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), except beef, veal, bovine offal and dried beef (73 lines, U.S. note 52(b), 9903.05.86). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese goods 12.5% in total when the base rate is lower. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). Pork, lamb, poultry, game and cured meat from these economies pay the duty.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil — beef exempt
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). Beef, veal and bovine offal are on the exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) stacks on top for other meat, which then pays 37.5%.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply to Canadian and Mexican meat.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs — beef exempt
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Beef, veal, bovine offal and dried beef were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); pork, lamb, poultry and other meat paid it. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Extra 80,000 t beef quota for Argentina
changes.detail: Proclamation 11010 adds 80,000 t of in-quota lean beef trimmings of Argentina for 2026 (on top of its 20,000 t), in four 20,000 t quarterly tranches from February 13 to December 31, 2026, first come, first served (9903.54.01).

changes.title: Beef quota: 13,000 t for the UK, "other countries" cut to 52,005 t
changes.detail: USTR moved 13,000 t of the "other countries or areas" beef quota into a new country-specific quota for the United Kingdom, under the U.S.–UK Economic Prosperity Deal. Brazil, Japan, the EU and other suppliers without their own allocation now share 52,005 t instead of 65,005 t.

changes.title: "Product of USA" labels now require U.S. born, raised, slaughtered and processed
changes.detail: From January 1, 2026, meat and poultry labels may carry a voluntary "Product of USA" or "Made in the USA" claim only if the animal was born, raised, slaughtered and processed in the United States (9 CFR 412.3). Imported meat that is cut or packed in the United States can no longer use the claim.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 duty: 10% from 2027, 15% from 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a phased duty on products of Nicaragua (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It does not apply to goods that originate under CAFTA-DR (U.S. note 29), which covers most of the $444M of Nicaraguan meat — almost all beef.

changes.title: Beef taken out of the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 added beef, veal, bovine offal and dried beef to the reciprocal-tariff exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii), 9903.01.32), for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. EST on November 13, 2025. Pork, lamb, poultry and other meat stayed subject until all IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Brazilian beef freed from the 40% IEEPA duty
changes.detail: Executive Order 14361 removed beef and other agricultural products from the 40% duty on Brazil (9903.01.77; exemption list 9903.01.81), effective for goods entered from November 13, 2025. Together with EO 14360 this ended an over-quota rate of 76.4% (26.4% + 10% + 40%) on Brazilian beef.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 (signed July 30, 2025) added 40% on goods of Brazil from August 6, 2025, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Beef was not exempt until November 13, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). USMCA-qualifying meat stayed exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx) on all meat, including beef until November 13, 2025; Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Foot-and-mouth disease: pork and ruminant meat from Hungary and Slovakia restricted
changes.detail: After foot-and-mouth disease was confirmed, APHIS restricted animal commodities from or through Hungary and Slovakia (from February 2, 2025) and Austria (from February 24, 2025): unprocessed pork and ruminant products arriving as cargo are prohibited with limited exceptions; processed products need APHIS-compliant treatment or must be commercially cooked and shelf-stable. U.S. meat imports from Hungary fell from $12.1M in 2024 to $3.0M in 2025.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. meat imports rose from **$15.27B in 2024 to $18.16B in 2025** (+18.9%), and almost all of the growth is **beef**: headings 0201 and 0202 went from $10.76B to $13.42B (+24.7%) and are now 74% of the chapter. Australia (+27.8%), Uruguay (+47.1%), Argentina (+50.4%) and Paraguay (from $96M to $291M) grew fastest; pork (0203) was flat at $1.52B and lamb and goat meat (0204) rose 11.5% to $1.72B.

The pull came from the U.S. side. The Administration's own beef proclamations describe a herd at its lowest level in 75 years after drought and wildfires, record ground-beef prices, and a 4% drop in U.S. beef output forecast for 2026 — which is why it widened the beef quota in 2026 (80,000 t more for Argentina, 300,000 t more for lean trimmings).

Tariffs slowed little of it. Beef from most countries paid the 10% reciprocal duty from April 2025 until November 13, 2025, and Brazilian over-quota beef briefly paid 76.4%, yet Brazil still grew 21.9%. Since November 13, 2025 beef has been exempt from every new duty. Animal disease mattered more for small suppliers: imports from Hungary fell from $12.1M to $3.0M after APHIS restricted pork from foot-and-mouth-affected countries in February 2025. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on meat depends on **what it is and where it comes from**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

**Beef and bovine offal pay no extra duty from any of the 60 Section 301 economies**, so for beef the base rate decides: 4.4¢/kg (or Free with an FTA or USMCA claim) inside the quota, 26.4% above it — except Australian beef, which stays Free above its quota under the Australia FTA unless the 17.1% price-based safeguard applies. Everything else from those economies pays the Section 301 duty since July 24, 2026: **10% in total for the EU**, **+10% for Canada, Mexico and Argentina**, **+12.5% for Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, Chile and Nicaragua**, +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying meat from Canada and Mexico enters free, and Paraguay — outside the 60 — pays only the base rate.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Meat into the U.S.: FSIS & APHIS Rules, Beef Quota & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 02) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The documents and rules for each HTS Chapter 02 line — USDA FSIS eligibility and import inspection, APHIS disease rules, FDA prior notice for game meat, Fish & Wildlife — and the legal ways to pay less: the beef quota, USMCA and FTA claims, Chapter 98, drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For meat the first question is not the rate but **whether it can enter at all**. Beef, pork, lamb, goat, horse meat and poultry need a country and a plant that USDA FSIS has approved, a foreign inspection certificate, and FSIS reinspection at an approved import establishment; APHIS disease rules can close a region overnight. Game meat, rabbit and frogs' legs fall under FDA instead, and wildlife rules add Fish & Wildlife.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: **enter beef inside the quota** (4.4¢/kg instead of 26.4%), **claim USMCA or an FTA**, or use a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Enter beef inside the tariff-rate quota
levers.saves: The difference between 26.4% of value and 4.4¢/kg — about $39,000 on a $150,000 container of 25 t of beef
levers.appliesTo: Beef lines of 0201 and 0202 "described in additional U.S. note 3" (in quota) vs. the "Other" over-quota lines
levers.document: Entry under the in-quota subheading while your country's quantity is open: Australia 378,214 t, New Zealand 213,402 t, Argentina 20,000 t (+80,000 t of lean trimmings in 2026), Uruguay 20,000 t, United Kingdom 13,000 t, everyone else 52,005 t (+300,000 t of lean trimmings, September 1 – November 30, 2026). Canada and Mexico have no limit.
levers.caveat: Quotas fill first come, first served; the "other countries or areas" quantity can fill early in the year. Check CBP's quota status before shipping — once a quota is full, the same beef pays 26.4%.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on meat from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 26.4% on beef) and the 10% Section 301 duty on non-beef meat
levers.appliesTo: All 166 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim a free trade agreement (Australia, Chile, CAFTA-DR and others)
levers.saves: The base rate — for beef and bovine offal the whole duty, including over-quota beef from Chile, Peru, Colombia, Korea or CAFTA-DR countries; for other meat the Section 301 duty stays
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose Special column lists the agreement (AU, BH, CL, CO, IL, JO, KR, MA, OM, P, PA, PE, SG)
levers.document: A claim on the entry with the agreement's certification or origin information — for example Chile (19 CFR 10.410, 10.411), CAFTA-DR (19 CFR 10.583) or Australia (19 CFR 10.703). Australian over-quota beef is claimed under 9822.04.01–9822.04.03.
levers.caveat: An FTA claim does not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty on non-beef meat (U.S. note 52(a)). Australia's FTA beef is Free up to 71,695 t in 2026 and then Free unless the price-based safeguard (17.1%) applies.

levers.title: Certify processed in-quota beef as "high-quality beef cuts"
levers.saves: 4% instead of 10% of value on processed in-quota beef cuts
levers.document: Certification before export by an official of the exporting country's government that the cuts meet the USDA specifications for Prime or Choice beef.
levers.caveat: Only for "processed" cuts entered in quota; ground, diced, stew or skewered beef does not qualify.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the facts fit
levers.saves: The base rate and the Section 301 duty: the provision below is Free
levers.appliesTo: U.S. meat that was exported and comes back without being processed abroad (for example a rejected export shipment)
levers.document: Proof that the goods are U.S. products returned unchanged, and FSIS clearance of the returned U.S.-inspected product.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 entries (U.S. note 52(a)). Returned meat must also meet 9 CFR 327.17.

provisions.text: Products of the United States returned after export without being advanced in value or improved in condition abroad

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported meat is exported again
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on meat that is exported or used to make exported products
levers.appliesTo: Any line, when the imported meat (or substitutable meat under the same 8-digit subheading) is exported
levers.document: A drawback claim with import and export records linking the two.
levers.caveat: Not every duty is eligible for drawback; confirm with CBP which duties on your entry can be refunded before pricing on it.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the classification (processed vs. not, in-quota line, game vs. poultry) before the goods arrive
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product and the intended entry.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a different product may need its own.

seo.title: Meat & Beef Tariffs FAQ: Australia, Brazil, Argentina, Canada Beef, Lamb, HS Codes (HTS Ch. 02) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people actually search about meat tariffs: the tariff on beef from Australia, Brazil, Argentina and Canada, the beef import quota, lamb from New Zealand, HS codes for beef, chicken and pork, and how to import meat into the U.S.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing meat into the U.S. — beef tariffs by country, the beef quota, lamb, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Beef, veal and bovine offal are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (and were exempt from the Section 122 surcharge and, from November 13, 2025, the IEEPA duties): for beef the base rate and the quota decide the cost — 4.4¢/kg in quota, 26.4% above it, Free with USMCA or most FTAs.

Other meat — pork, lamb, poultry, cured ham — from the 60 Section 301 economies pays an extra duty since July 24, 2026: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +37.5% for Brazil. USMCA-qualifying meat from Canada and Mexico enters free.
In 2026 the beef quota grew: 80,000 t more for Argentina and 300,000 t more for lean trimmings (September 1 – November 30). And no meat enters without USDA FSIS approval of the country and plant.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on imported beef and meat right now?
faqs.answer: Beef has only its base rate: 4.4¢/kg inside the tariff-rate quota and 26.4% above it, Free with USMCA or most FTA claims. Beef, veal and bovine offal are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)), were exempt from the 10% Section 122 surcharge, and were taken out of the IEEPA reciprocal and Brazil duties on November 13, 2025. Other meat — pork, lamb, poultry, cured ham — pays its base rate plus a Section 301 duty of 10% to 12.5% (37.5% for Brazil) if it comes from one of the 60 economies, since July 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on Australian beef?
searchedAs: tariff on australian beef to usa
faqs.answer: Usually zero. Australian beef enters free under the Australia FTA within Australia's 378,214 t quota, then free for another 71,695 t in 2026, and beyond that free unless the price-based safeguard (17.1%) is triggered. Beef is exempt from the 12.5% Section 301 duty on Australian goods. The 10% reciprocal duty that applied from April 2025 was lifted for beef on November 13, 2025. Australia was the largest supplier in 2025, with $3.76B of beef.

faqs.question: What is the current tariff on Brazilian beef?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on brazilian beef
faqs.answer: 4.4¢/kg inside the quota and 26.4% above it — the base rate only. Brazil uses the 52,005 t "other countries or areas" quota and, until November 30, 2026, the extra 300,000 t for lean beef trimmings. Beef is exempt from both Section 301 duties on Brazil (25% and 12.5%). The 40% IEEPA duty and the 10% reciprocal duty, which pushed over-quota Brazilian beef to 76.4% from August 6, 2025, were lifted for beef on November 13, 2025. Other Brazilian meat, such as pork, pays its base rate plus 37.5%.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on Argentine beef, and how big is the Argentina beef quota?
faqs.answer: Argentina has a 20,000 t yearly beef quota and, for 2026 only, an extra 80,000 t of lean beef trimmings (Proclamation 11010, in quarterly tranches of 20,000 t from February 13 to December 31, 2026). In quota the rate is 4.4¢/kg; above it 26.4%. Beef is exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Argentine goods. Imports of Argentine meat rose 50% to $343M in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a U.S. tariff on Canadian beef?
searchedAs: is there a us tariff on canadian beef
what is the current tariff on canadian beef
faqs.answer: Not on USMCA-qualifying beef, which enters free with no quota limit. Canadian beef that does not qualify pays only the base rate (4.4¢/kg on most lines) — beef is exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian goods, and the 2026 Section 338 duties on Canada do not cover meat. The 35% IEEPA duty ended on February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $2.81B of beef to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Mexican beef?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on mexican beef
faqs.answer: No, if it qualifies for USMCA: Mexican beef then enters free, with no quota limit. Non-qualifying beef pays the base rate only, since beef is exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Mexican goods. The 25% IEEPA duty ended on February 24, 2026. Mexico was the No. 3 beef supplier in 2025 ($2.18B). The screwworm border closures apply to live cattle, not to meat.

faqs.question: How does the U.S. beef import quota work?
faqs.answer: It is a tariff-rate quota, not a ban. Each year a set quantity enters at the low in-quota rate (4.4¢/kg; 4% or 10% on processed cuts): Australia 378,214 t, New Zealand 213,402 t, Argentina and Uruguay 20,000 t each, the United Kingdom 13,000 t and all other countries 52,005 t together; Canada and Mexico have no limit. Beef entered after a quota fills pays 26.4% (additional U.S. note 3 to Chapter 2) — except Australian beef with an FTA claim, which stays Free (71,695 t more in 2026, then Free unless the 17.1% price-based safeguard applies). For 2026, Argentina got 80,000 t more and lean trimmings from other countries 300,000 t more.

faqs.question: What are lean beef trimmings, and why is more being imported?
faqs.answer: Lean boneless beef that is blended with fattier U.S. trimmings to make ground beef. They enter under 0201.30.50 and 0202.30.50. To lower ground-beef prices, Proclamation 11059 opened an extra 300,000 t of in-quota lean trimmings (4.4¢/kg instead of 26.4%) for countries without their own allocation, from September 1 to November 30, 2026, in three 100,000 t tranches, on top of the 80,000 t for Argentina.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on lamb from New Zealand or Australia?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on lamb
faqs.answer: Lamb has a base rate of 0.7¢/kg (Free for Australia with an FTA claim), but since July 24, 2026 both countries pay a 12.5% Section 301 duty on lamb, mutton and goat meat (9903.05.23, 9903.05.57). A $180,000 container of New Zealand lamb legs owes about $22,640. The U.S. imported $1.72B of sheep and goat meat in 2025, almost all from these two countries.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on goat meat?
faqs.answer: The base rate on goat meat (0204.50) is Free, but goat meat from a Section 301 economy pays that country's extra duty — 12.5% for Australia, the main supplier. The U.S. imported $164M of goat meat in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for beef?
faqs.answer: Fresh or chilled beef is heading 0201 and frozen beef 0202; each splits into carcasses (.10), bone-in cuts (.20) and boneless (.30). The U.S. lines then split by whether the beef enters inside the quota (4.4¢/kg) or above it (26.4%). Frozen boneless beef, 0202.30, was the largest product in the chapter in 2025 ($6.32B). Beef offal is 0206, dried or salted beef 0210.20, and beef jerky and other prepared beef are in Chapter 16.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for chicken meat?
faqs.answer: Chicken is 0207.11–0207.14: whole birds fresh (0207.11) or frozen (0207.12) at 8.8¢/kg, and cuts and offal — breasts, wings, feet, livers — fresh (0207.13) or frozen (0207.14) at 17.6¢/kg. Turkey is 0207.24–0207.27, duck 0207.41–0207.45. Poultry needs a country and plant FSIS has approved for poultry.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for pork?
faqs.answer: Fresh or chilled pork is 0203.11–0203.19 and frozen 0203.21–0203.29. Unprocessed cuts, including bellies (0203.19.40.10), are Free; "processed" cuts such as spare ribs made ready for retail (0203.19.20.10) are 1.4¢/kg. Bacon is 0210.12 and cured ham 0210.11 (1.4¢/kg). The Section 301 duty for the country of origin applies on top.

faqs.question: Can you import meat into the U.S., and what do you need?
searchedAs: can you import meat into the us
faqs.answer: Yes, commercially, if the exporting country and plant are eligible with USDA FSIS (9 CFR 327.2; 381.196 for poultry). Each shipment needs a foreign inspection certificate (9 CFR 327.4), an import inspection application and FSIS reinspection at an approved import establishment (9 CFR 327.5, 327.6). APHIS disease rules can bar meat from regions with foot-and-mouth disease, swine fevers or avian influenza (9 CFR part 94). Game meat, rabbit and frogs' legs fall under FDA prior notice instead.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import its beef from?
faqs.answer: $13.42B of beef in 2025, up from $10.76B in 2024: Australia $3.76B (28%), Canada $2.81B, Mexico $2.18B, New Zealand $1.29B, Brazil $1.26B and Uruguay $0.82B, followed by Nicaragua, Argentina and Paraguay. Beef was 74% of all U.S. meat imports ($18.16B).
